name: FC Barcelona 1990-94 (Cruyff's Dream Team)
scopeNote: Cruyff's Barcelona from the 1990/91 season to the 1994 European Cup final in Athens (18 May 1994). Sources use the term Dream Team and a 3-4-3 (in possession, 4-3-3 off the ball), Total Football lineage from Michels/Ajax. Start date 1990-09-01 (first La Liga match, away to Espanyol) comes from a search summary of the club chronology, not read on a page; the 1990 Supercopa vs Real Madrid may be earlier. Many tactical sources describe 1988-96 generally; facts with eventDate 1991/92 are general descriptions of the Dream Team years, filed under the 1992 title season because the validator rejects ranges. Undated stated-view quotes carry the earliest publication date found (not original date). Marking scheme (zonal vs man) not found for this team.
openQuestions: Start date 1990-09-01 is from a search summary (club chronology), unverified on a page; the 1990 Supercopa vs Real Madrid (Stoichkov's Clasico debut) may precede it.
Zonal vs man-marking: no source read describes Barcelona's marking scheme; one search hit (fussballcoach.substack.com) says Cruyff used 30 zones but was not mined.

Base shape: Coaches' Voice says 3-4-3 in possession becoming 4-3-3 off the ball; 1994 final used a 4-3-3 with two centre-backs; a search summary claimed 3-4-3 was used mainly against two forwards (unverified).
Several tactical sources are retrospectives; the Cruyff quotes are cited as attributed because no primary dated source was found.
Zubizarreta set-piece anecdote and Alexanko booing refer to 1988/89, outside the period, so left unverified.
Claims of 'high press' in 90min/Goal are generic; Coaches' Voice says the team rarely counter-pressed intensely.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: If opponents positioned themselves in a low block, the build-up would always start from the goalkeeper. With the ball at his feet, Zubizarreta would have the options of playing into Koeman or the midfield pivot to start building up the team’s progression.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: In situations when the opposing team played a high pressing game, goalkeeper Andoni Zubizarreta could play a medium-range pass into the defensive pivot or play long towards one of the wingers. If the ball was with Koeman, the long switch was a common tactic.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Possession of the ball by itself did not interest Cruyff. He wanted his players to understand that, in order to keep it and move towards the opponents’ goal, the ball had to be moved and moved and moved.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: By encouraging one of his wingers or full-backs inside, he wanted his team to maintain very close passing lines, thus shortening the distance between players.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: With the exception of the full-backs, the rest of the players in Cruyff’s system were not expected to make long horizontal or vertical movements when the team was in possession. Equally, his teams rarely executed a high or intense counter-press after losing the ball

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: his teams rarely executed a high or intense counter-press after losing the ball – this gave the opposition both time and space on the counter-attack, which often left Cruyff’s defensive line vulnerable on defensive transitions. It was no coincidence that his Barcelona team conceded so many goals.

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: The role played by the full-backs was fundamental, however, as this allowed Cruyff to widen the pitch. Ferrer and Sergi advanced as traditional wide players down the lines, which allowed the wingers – most commonly Hristo Stoichkov and Andoni Goikoetxea – to move into more central areas

sources.title: Johan Cruyff: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

statedView.quote: Football basically consists of two things. First, when you have the ball, you must be able to pass it properly. Second, when the ball is passed to you, you must be able to control it.
If you have four men defending two strikers, you only have six against eight in the middle of the field: there’s no way you can win that battle. We had to put a defender further forward.
I was criticised for playing three at the back, but that’s the most idiotic thing I’ve ever heard... I much prefer to win 5-4 than 1-0.
It’s a basic concept: when you dominate the ball, you move well. You have what the opposition don’t, and therefore they can’t score.
We're more complete, competitive and experienced than at Wembley. Milan are nothing out of this world. They base their game on defence, we base ours on attack.
It was not that we played badly, it was that we did not play at all.
If you don’t lose the ball in the build-up, it’s very difficult to be counter-attacked.
